stories.title: Efforts continue to restart public sector pay talks
stories.summary: Trade unions and Government representatives will continue engagement today with an independent group in a bid to find a pathway to talks on the ongoing public sector pay dispute. Meetings with a Government-appointed group, chaired by Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) Chair Kevin Foley, were adjourned yesterday evening and will resume this morning. On Monday, unions announced plans for a 24-hour strike on Thursday 12 November. They have accused the Government of failing to make a credible offer on pay. It is understood unions rejected a Government offer of pay increases worth 7.75% over two and a half years. General Secretary of Fórsa and Chair of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions' Public Services Committee Kevin Callinan said they are looking for a better deal than the last public sector pay agreement.

stories.title: 40% of income spent on rent in areas around Dublin - CSO
stories.summary: More than a third of tenants living in the South Dublin Co Council area spent over 40% of their disposable income on rent, according to the Central Statistics Office. The study, based on 2024 figures, showed that in Fingal, Louth and Wicklow a third of tenants spent more than 40% on their disposable income on rent. The study analysed the "rent burden" by measuring the median rent as a percentage of disposable income for tenants. The local electoral areas with the highest rent burdens were Tallaght South at 33.7%, Balbriggan at 32.9%, Ongar at 27.1% and Ballyfermot-Drimnagh at 30.5%. The areas with the lowest burdens were Ballinamore in Co Leitrim at 14.9%, Lismore in Co Waterford at 14.5% and Belmullet in Co Mayo at 10.3%. Almost three-quarter of tenants had employee earnings as their primary source of income.

stories.summary: There are fears of job losses at laboratory testing service Enfer Medical in Naas, Co Kildare. The Department of Enterprise said it received a collective redundancy notification from the company last month. "The Department received a notification of proposed collective redundancies from Enfer Medical Limited on 6 October 2026," a spokesperson said. "Any further queries should be directed to the company," they added. Enfer Medical said it would not be commenting on a report today from Kildare radio station KFM which said the company is set to cease operations this month. Part of the Enfer Group, Enfer Medical describes itself as a leading clinical laboratory.

stories.title: Nearly 90m displaced facing severe climate risks - UN
stories.summary: Three-quarters of the world's displaced people live in countries facing severe exposure to climate-related hazards, the United Nations said, calling for urgent action to protect them. Days before the COP31 climate conference starts in Turkey, a UN refugee agency report said nearly 90 million refugees and other forcibly displaced people faced severe risks linked to a warming planet. "Refugees face a double injustice," said Anton Leis Garcia, UNHCR's assistant high commissioner for operations. "Forced to flee conflicts they did not cause, they are now on the frontlines of a climate crisis they have contributed least to." People forced to flee conflict, violence and persecution find themselves in places grappling with severe droughts, deadly floods and extreme heat, the organisation pointed out. Climate change was also increasingly threatening the prospect of lasting solutions for displaced people, UNHCR said.

stories.title: New boss Trant seeking characters to rekindle Dubs 'aura'
stories.summary: There's that famous, oft-quoted line from John Maughan - well, one of many - as he dragged the Mayo men's footballers up by their boot straps back towards respectability in the late 1990s. Maughan - an army man from head to toe and eminently quotable - had a preference for a particular type of Mayo footballer. The Crossmolina man had no time for those who merely liked to be seen to be county players. He wanted people who needed it. During his first stint in charge of the county, from 1995 to 1999, he led them to two All-Ireland finals and somewhere along the line declared that he "didn't just want football players", he wanted "lads who would eat grass to play for Mayo". Trant was the Dubs' last line of defence during a period of unparralleled success in the 2010s that delivered four straight Brendan Martin Cups from 2017 to 2020 in a time when the Girls in Blue reached eight consecutive All-Ireland finals. Indeed, an accidental goalkeeper to an extent when thrust in between the sticks for a minor match with Dublin at age 16 - "apparently it was John Caffrey's idea to stick me in goal" - Trant finds herself in possession of the bainisteoir's bib somewhat ahead of schedule. Having been involved in coaching since the early days of her playing career - initially at St Finian's where she led the club's first ever juvenile girls team to an Under-14 championship in 2013 while still on the inter-county Under-21 panel - Trant spent last year as a coach with the Dublin side jointly managed by Paul Casey and Derek Murray.
stories.rssSummary: The four-in-a-row winning goalkeeper has enjoyed a speedy rise up the coaching ranks within Dublin football as she takes over the reins from Paul Casey and Derek Murray heading into the 2027 season.

stories.title: Sounding Ireland: how radio became the nation's new confessional
stories.summary: We cannot know what future generations will make of the last half-century's sharing of the profoundly personal on air by people whose public lives are well known to us. It seems that in an increasingly secular society, the media – broadcast and more recently online – has become the country’s new confessional. The appeal of such radio is undeniable. Before the broadcast the presenter advises on the sensitivity of the subject and the circumstances of the recording or live interview. Many listeners cite these interviews as the most memorable and impactful radio experiences of their lives. Perhaps there is some comfort, or some thread of connection formed by hearing that other people’s lives are as complex and fragile as our own. It can also be cathartic for the guest to bare their soul to a nation they have a real relationship with. Sometimes such radio catches the intensity of life on the cusp of dying. When Marian Finucane met Nuala O’Faolain for lunch in 2008, O’Faolain told her friend she was dying. Marian later said that unbelievable though it was, once Nuala told her about her cancer, they started talking about doing an interview. Marian had interviewed Nuala a few times since the publication of her memoir, Are You Somebody? She knew that 'being interviewed live provided [Nuala] with an important means of understanding herself. It was as if answering questions under pressure marshalled all her considerable gifts, allowing her to speak with her wonderful blend of candour, wit and passion.’ And she did. They were recorded within days of the unedited broadcast of the conversation; the stop-starts told their own truth. O’Faolain talked about getting her diagnosis in the emergency department of a New York hospital. She had built her life there and now that life – with her ‘beloved room’, her friends, writing and Ireland – was suddenly reduced to ‘wretchedness, such sourness with life, and fear …’ She wondered ‘how we all get away with our unthinkingness’ and suggested a record ‘that you might play at the end, I know you don’t go playing records, particularly for dying people but still …’ The song was ‘Thíos i Lár an Ghleanna’ (Down in the Middle of the Glen), sung by Albert Fry: ‘Is a Íosa i lár na bhflaithis, tabhair arais an oíche aréir’. Marian Finucane finished the interview by playing the song for O’Faolain. In 2015 Miriam O’Callaghan’s guest on her Sunday morning show was Leo Varadkar. It was his thirty-sixth birthday. She had often interviewed him about policies and crises but said this was ‘not one of those interviews’. During the live interview, he came out as gay to the Irish public – the first serving Irish government minister to do so. The upcoming marriage equality referendum, legislation on surrogacy and whether to change the ban on gay and bisexual men donating blood were coming down the line. As minister for health, Varadkar said he wanted to be honest with people about who he was but also wanted to be ‘an equal citizen in my own country, the country in which I am a member of government and now I am not’. stories.title: Meet four of the characters from The Galway Bay Murders
stories.summary: When the body of a young woman is discovered on a Conamara bog, visiting NYPD detective Lieutenant Nora Savage (Star Trek: Voyager's Kate Mulgrew) and new Dublin arrival Detective Eddie McDonagh (Love/Hate's John Connors) are paired for the investigation by Superintendent Pearce Folan (Colm Meaney). A twist-filled mystery ensues as Nora and Eddie follow the leads to Free Farm, the global farming and scientific research organisation whose headquarters are nearby. Below, four more stars of The Galway Bay Murders - James Ó'Quinn, Declan Rodgers, India Mullen, and Cillian O'Sullivan - profile their characters and tease what's ahead. "Ronan is one of the young members at Free Farm," says James Ó Quinn. "I suppose Ronan is somebody who has been given a second chance at Free Farm with this new life. It's basically one big family of climate-conscious farmers. He's had a bit of a rocky past, and now he's in this new world where he has a family; he has people that he cares about, and they all care about each other. And then all of a sudden this world of his gets flipped upside down and he deals with the consequences of that. "Once it gets into it, it takes it from this murder that's happened and then from that, not that everybody's a suspect, but you grow into... Suddenly this bigger, wider world is opened up through that and through the process of the investigation. We've got this almost, like, an epic story that you wouldn't think is going on in here."

stories.title: Ireland's Fittest Family: Meet tonight's competitors
stories.summary: Ireland's Fittest Family is back with more thrills, more fierce competition and an exciting brand new location thrown into the mix. Now in its 14th season, the beloved show is back with coaches Anna Geary, Donncha O'Callaghan, Davy Fitzgerald, Ellen Keane, Michael Darragh MacAuley and reigning champion Andrew Trimble. Kicking off in the historic Haulbowline Navy Base, the Heats will unfold over three weeks. Each week, two coaches will go head-to-head, each with two families. For week two, it's the turn of Michael Darragh MacAuley to take on Davy Fitzgerald. Mam Kathy-Ann, 49, is a PE Teacher and TY Coordinator. She played badminton and hockey but gave it up two years ago and now does her own fitness routine and swims once a week. The staff in her school convinced her to sign up this year - her children have been wanting to do it for the last five years! Daughter Jessica, 14, is a new addition to the team as her older sister Hannah was the family's first pick but due to scheduling conflicts Hannah is unable to compete. Jessica is very excited to step up! She is a 2nd Year student at the school that Kathy-Ann teaches at.

stories.title: Taoiseach to take part in Enniskillen Remembrance event
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin will lay a laurel wreath at the war memorial in Enniskillen in Co Fermanagh this morning as part of Remembrance Sunday events taking place across the UK. The ceremony in Enniskillen also remembers the 12 people killed in an IRA bomb attack on the Remembrance event in the town in 1987. It comes as Sinn Féin deputy leader and Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O’Neill will not attend the ceremony at the Cenotaph in Belfast this year because the DUP has blocked her from acting in an official capacity as part of its response to the Orange Order’s Drumcree parade dispute. Sinn Féin Lord Mayor of Belfast, Rois-Maire Donnelly, will take part in the Remembrance ceremony and lay a wreath. Michelle O’Neill laid a laurel wreath at the Cenotaph in Belfast for the past two years but won’t do so this year because it was a joint invitation along with deputy first minister Emma Little Pengelly of the DUP and her party has banned any joint engagements. The DUP took the action in response to the First Minister’s participation in an unlawful protest that blocked the proposed route of an Orange Order parade along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown on the last Sunday in September.

stories.title: Dignam sends UCD back to the top flight at Drogs' expense
stories.summary: Goals from Ciarán Behan and Louis Dignam saw UCD dramatically upset the odds and regain their place in the SSE Airtricity Premier Division at Drogheda United's expense. Few would have given College a chance when they fell behind to an early Mark Doyle header but the Belfield side were full value for a more-than-merited win at Tallaght Stadium. The Students will return to the top tier following a three-year absence, with Dignam’s spectacular second-half winner the pick of the bunch. The first chance of note fell in the 12th minute as Conor Kane found his namesake Keeley in the box but the defender could not steer his header on target. That was rectified shortly after as Alfie Bates swung a cross in from a deep position and this time Mark Doyle’s flicked effort beat Dara Kavanagh in the UCD goal. That should have been the impetus for the Premier Division side to take control but instead it was the Students who took command of the encounter.

stories.title: Gunman 'fascinated by far-right' kills six in Krakow
stories.summary: Six people were killed and at least 15 injured when a gunman opened fire in the landmark historic centre of Poland's second city of Krakow, in the country's deadliest shooting in decades. Three bodies - of two women and a man - were later found at the suspect's home, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, adding there was "much to suggest that they are members of the (suspect's) immediate family". Mr Tusk also announced Poland would hold two days of mourning over the shooting that he called an act of "terrorism". Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the gunman appeared to be "fascinated by far-right ideologies". A British national was among the killed, according to Polish police chief, Marek Boron, and five foreigners were among the wounded in hospital, the authorities said. "Two people who have not yet been identified," Mr Boron said referring to the victims killed.

stories.title: Power shoots 65 to fly up the leaderboard in Mexico
stories.summary: Séamus Power jumped up 44 places at the World Wide Technology Championship in Los Cabos in Mexico after posting a third-round seven-under-par 65. The Waterford native squeezed inside the cut on Friday, but a blemish-free round that included two eagles, sees him move to 12-under par, nine shots off leader Ben James (-21) of the United States who will take a four-stroke lead over compatriot Ryan Gerard into Sunday. Only Michael Kim (63) enjoyed a lower round than the 39-year-old Power, who holed out from 80 yards at the par-5 sixth hole. Starting at the 10th, the two-time winner on the PGA Tour drained a 16ft putt at the 13th for his first birdie of the day. In a steady back nine, he exorcised the demons of the 18th from Friday, where he suffered a double-bogey, with a straight-forward birdie. That began a purple patch where Power picked up seven shots in the following seven holes. An eagle at the first owed much to a superb second shot, stitching the ball to within six feet of the flag. Power's iron play was coming to the fore, creating scoring opportunities, which he took at the third and fourth before his shot of the day came at the 593-yard par-5 sixth.

stories.title: PSNI still struggling to recruit Catholics, 25 years on
stories.summary: One of a small proportion of Catholic officers in the RUC, a police force distrusted and disliked by many nationalists in Northern Ireland throughout the Troubles. At its height, 8% of those in its ranks were from a Catholic background. He joined in September 1994, a month after the Provisional IRA had declared a ceasefire. That ended in February 1996, with the bombing of Canary Wharf in London, and was restored in July the following year. "I always had this vocation that I wanted to help people, and for me, at that time, policing was the practical option for me to do that," he says. "I had the full support of my family, and it's important to say that you need the support of your family, and the backing of your peers and friends. I had that backing." He felt more at threat because of his Catholic background as the IRA was keen to prevent people from his community supporting or joining a police force they characterised as the enemy.
stories.rssSummary: A quarter of a century after its birth, the proportion of Catholic officers in the PSNI has plateaued, rather than increasing, as the architects of the reform had intended.

stories.title: Drama at the death as O'Neill lands late Cross winner
stories.summary: A 63rd-minute two-pointer from Rian O'Neill saw Crossmaglen come from 11 down to defeat Cavan champions Gowna in a dramatic contest at Kingspan Breffni. In perfect conditions with very little wind, Gowna played outstanding football in the first half but a wasteful Cross ground them down and the Cavanmen, who were unhappy with some decisions in the second half, wilted. Cavan’s dreadful record in the competition had been well-advertised – Gowna themselves, in 2002, were the last Breffni champions other than Cavan Gaels to win a match – but Cavan sides had come agonisingly close to a win on numerous occasions so there was a degree of optimism within the county. Yet Crossmaglen’s reputation preceded them. They may not have had a win in Ulster since 2018 but they stand alone at the top of the provincial roll of honour with 11 titles. The chief questions pre-match were whether Gowna could contain Cross’s stellar forward line and inflict damage at the other end. As always, the midfield battle was expected to be crucial and that’s where this match was chiefly won and lost. Gowna were strong in that sector in the first half but Crossmaglen, a team who thrive on momentum, took control on kick-outs in the second half as their nerve in tight contests came to the fore again.

stories.title: FG pledges 'penalties' for avoiding back-to-work services
stories.summary: Tánaiste Simon Harris has pledged to penalise long-term unemployed people who refuse to engage with services to get them back to work. The Fine Gael leader told his party's Ard Fheis in Cork, that it was not acceptable for people to be out of work at a time of full employment, adding that "the dole is a safety net, not a way of life". In his main speech this evening, Mr Harris said: "At a time of full employment, it is simply not acceptable for any person to remain on the Live Register year after year after year." "We need a renewed focus on intensive engagement with the long-term unemployed - tackling barriers, creating opportunities and getting people into work. "And let me be clear, for those who refuse to engage, there will be penalties." Mr Harris also addressed the challenges posed by AI and the fear that it will displace many jobs - particularly entry level positions.

stories.title: Carrick not seeking assurances ahead of Villa's visit
stories.summary: Michael Carrick says he has not been given any further assurances about his Manchester United future heading into Sunday's critical Premier League match against Aston Villa and the international window that follows. In the wake of a hugely damaging 3-0 home loss to Bournemouth two weeks ago – a match many then expected to be Carrick’s last in charge – it was eventually communicated by United that their former captain would be given time to turn things around. But no scale was put on that and Carrick remains under pressure despite Tuesday night’s dramatic Champions League win over Roma, which saw United rally from a 2-0 half-time deficit to win 3-2 thanks to Bruno Fernandes’ twice-taken penalty and Matheus Cunha’s late brace. That result no doubt helped Carrick but did not paper over the cracks showing after the nine-match winless run that preceded it, with United having started this weekend hovering just above the relegation zone and entering it when Nottingham Forest beat Manchester City. Asked if he had been told for certain he would still be in charge beyond the weekend, Carrick said: "No, I’ve just carried on as absolute normal." And when asked if he was entering Sunday’s match with any feeling of uncertainty, Carrick added: "No, no. Whatever happens is going to happen in terms of the game and we’ve got to prepare right, looking forward to it."

stories.title: Houthis say Saudi strikes kill 33 in Yemen
stories.summary: According to Houthi authorities, Saudi strikes killed 33 people, many of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, in one of the deadliest attacks reported since fighting resumed in the country. The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned group broke out again in July. The death toll from the Saudi-led coalition's strikes on Al-Shariya village, located east of Yemen's capital Sanaa, has risen to 33, with 39 people injured, Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi said in a post on X. The Houthis' Saba news agency yesterday said operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes". According to the near-final figures, the dead include 12 men, 8 women and 13 children, while the injured include 16 men, 10 women and 13 children," Mr Alasbahi said. The Iran-backed group's Al-Masirah TV broadcast footage, that it said was filmed in Al-Shariya, showed smoke rising from a site that had been struck, piles of debris and wounded people in hospital.

stories.title: Norris prevails in Sao Paulo rain to seize pole
stories.summary: Lando Norris conquered thunderstorms to claim pole for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix while Lewis Hamilton suffered an engine nightmare and will be forced to start Sunday's race from the back of the grid. In treacherous conditions at Interlagos, McLaren’s Norris rose to the top as he pipped compatriot George Russell on the track – but the Mercedes man will start seventh after a five-place grid drop. Kimi Antonelli, who deposed Norris as world champion last weekend, will be promoted to second while Liam Lawson – whose Racing Bulls seat remains in serious doubt – is a remarkable third on the grid. Russell was again furious with his Mercedes team, questioning why they asked him to back off on his final flying lap – believing that decision cost him pole. Ferrari announced ahead of final practice that both of their warring drivers would take 10-place grid drops, with Hamilton and Charles Leclerc changing their internal combustion engine to incur the penalty. But Hamilton immediately hit trouble. First he complained of vibrations from his new engine before having to come in again with his car pouring smoke from the back.

stories.title: After 15 years in power, what is Fine Gael in 2026?
stories.summary: After 15 years in power and 11 years in some form of partnership with Fianna Fáil, many delegates at Fine Gael's Ard Fheis were pondering this question as members met in Cork. Indeed, the group set up by Simon Harris when he took over the reins in April 2024 released its report this week concluding that many did not believe Fine Gael had a clear identity. And that theme was picked up by delegates at the discussion on the Commission for Renewal report. One member spoke about the fear of being "consumed into Fianna Fáil". Another agreed that he was "not convinced that we have articulated our core values". And another delegate insisted that Fine Gael should proudly declare itself as the Christian Democrat centre right party she believed it is at its core, adding that it should not "pivot to the left". And perhaps this is the essence of the dilemma for Fine Gael as it grapples with the difficult process of attempting to renew as a party when it has been in government for such a lengthy period.

stories.title: European wrap: Mbappe helps Real Madrid overcome Valencia
stories.summary: Kylian Mbappe scored his 17th goal of the season to help Real Madrid secure an eighth straight victory with a 3-0 La Liga win at Valencia. Captain Fede Valverde broke the deadlock at Mestalla with a powerful low finish into the bottom corner from 22 yards after 28 minutes. It was followed eight minutes later by a sweet first-time strike by Arda Guler, who fired home from a Jude Bellingham cross to score again in place of the suspended Vinicius Junior, before Mbappe wrapped up the points with a smart finish in the 75th minute. Madrid have moved on to 30 points with Barcelona, but Athletic Club remain outside of the European spots after Nico Williams' 84th-minute opener at Osasuna was cancelled out by a stoppage-time effort from Alejandro Catena. Former Bournemouth defender Illia Zabarnyi scored the only goal to help Ligue 1 leaders Paris Saint-Germain get the better of Troyes and Liam Rosenior’s Paris FC are second following a 1-0 triumph at Auxerre. Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane provided assists for Joshua Kimmich and Lennart Karl to help Bayern Munich return to winning ways in Bundesliga with a 2-1 victory at Mainz, while Borussia Dortmund picked up a 2-1 win over Elversberg.

stories.title: UFC's Dana White to meet Trump over press secretary offer
stories.summary: Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White said he will fly to Washington to discuss US President Donald Trump's offer to become White House press secretary. Mr Trump urged Mr White to take up the job in a Truth Social post on Saturday, naming several fighters from the mixed martial arts organisation who could serve as assistants. Speaking to reporters at an event in London, Mr White confirmed he would be meeting with the president. "I’m flying to DC right now and I’m sure we’ll have something to talk about after that." The president wrote on social media: "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States." He added: "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"

stories.title: What is COP31 and why does it matter?
stories.summary: Almost 200 countries are meeting in Turkey to negotiate how to tackle climate change at COP31. The summit is not primarily about persuading countries that climate change is happening. It is about persuading them to agree on what they are prepared to do about it, how quickly they will act, and who will pay. Here, Environment Correspondent George Lee provides a guide to what COP31 is, why it matters, what countries are arguing about, why agreement is so difficult and what the outcome could mean for Ireland. COP31 is the world's biggest annual gathering devoted to tackling climate change. Representatives of almost 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey, from 9 to 20 November to negotiate how the world should respond to rising global temperatures.

stories.title: Ireland to take on central role at COP31 climate summit
stories.summary: Ireland will take on a leading role in global climate negotiations when the COP31 summit begins in Turkey on Monday. It comes amid growing pressure on wealthy countries to deliver on commitments to tackle climate change. Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, Darragh O'Brien, has said the European Union needs to change its approach to developing countries following the sometimes-bitter disagreements at last year's summit in Brazil. However, Irish environmental organisations have warned that progress will depend on wealthy countries providing significantly more financial assistance to poorer nations, particularly through grants rather than loans. The COP31 summit, which takes place in Antalya from 9 - 20 November, will bring together representatives of almost every country in the world to negotiate measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and help countries adapt to the growing impacts of climate change. Ireland holds the rotating Presidency of the Council of the European Union and will play a central role, alongside the European Commission, in coordinating and leading the EU's negotiating effort.

stories.title: Adding up: The booming business of food additives
stories.summary: Food and drink additives have gotten something of a bad rap in recent times. Countless influencers and pseudo-nutritionists have built careers casting a cold eye on various ingredients lists' unpronounceables. But adding ingredients to what we consumer has been done for thousands of years – whether it’s to make what we eat and drink more appealing, or ensure it doesn’t spoil as quickly. But if we take a broader definition of food additive, you can also include the ingredients that are used to create fortified or enriched foods and drinks. They are two similar-but-slightly-different approaches to the same thing, where some form of nutrition is added under the guise of making it better for the people who consume it. With enriched foods, the term refers to returning the nutrients that are lost or removed in the process of making the product. You might enrich white flour, for example, by putting back the B vitamins and iron that are lost when you separate out the bran and the germ from the wheat.

stories.title: Israel president taps Eisenkot to form new government
stories.summary: Israel's president has announced he will task Gadi Eisenkot with forming the next government following last week's election, in what Benjamin Netanyahu's rivals see as a first step to remove the country's longest-serving prime minister. The opposition bloc led by Mr Eisenkot, a former military chief and political newcomer who has tried to appeal to secular and liberal Israelis, has opened the door to a once improbable alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jews, which could give it the numbers to form a coalition. President Isaac Herzog said that after consultations with all parties during the week, he would grant Mr Eisenkot the first chance to form a government after the 27 October election, in which neither side secured a majority in a country deeply polarised by Mr Netanyahu's hard-right rule and worn down by three years of war. The formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony tomorrow at the president's residence in Jerusalem, Mr Herzog's office said. Mr Eisenkot was recommended by parties representing 67 politicians as opposed to 46 for Mr Netanyahu's bloc. But the recommendations for Mr Eisenkot included members of Israel's Arab minority - whose seat haul soared in the election on the back of anger against Mr Netanyahu - and right-leaning segments of the opposition oppose relying on Arab votes.

stories.title: Call for clarity on existence of Ireland-UK airspace deal
stories.summary: Independent Senator Michael McDowell has called for clarity on whether Ireland has an agreement with the UK to defend its airspace, saying the public is entitled to know what arrangements are in place. He accepted that operational details could remain confidential for security reasons. "If that is the reality, the people of Ireland are entitled to know about it. It can’t be just kept secret," he said. European leaders are meeting in the capital next Thursday and Friday but the security operation around these events, which has been described as "unprecedented" will get under way two days before, on Tuesday 10 November. Mr McDowell said it was still unclear who was behind the threats. He said Ireland was relying on a French naval vessel to help secure Dublin’s airspace for the summit and that the Air Corps lacked aircraft capable of defending Irish airspace.

stories.title: Olympic medallist Muir recalls 'fierce fighter' Mageean
stories.summary: Olympic silver medallist Laura Muir has spoken of Ciara Mageean's 'fierce' determination on the track and "infectious energy" off it as tributes continue for the 1500m European champion. Irish Olympian and European champion runner Mageean died last week aged 34 after a 17-month battle with bowel cancer. Her funeral took place on Tuesday in her native Portaferry where mourners were told she was a bright light in the darkness who made the world a nicer place to call home. Muir and Mageean shared the 1500m start line 25 times in their careers on the track, with Muir getting the better of her Irish competitor on 19 of those occasions. "We have been running around in circles in a variety of competitions for a long time. Ciara always brought an infectious energy and would light up a room. She really embraced life." Mageean and Muir first crossed paths in 2012 at the popular British Milers Club race series in Manchester when 20-year-old Mageean went one nil up over her Scottish rival on their first meeting.

stories.title: FAI president stands by fulfillment of Israel fixtures
stories.summary: The President of the Football Association of Ireland Paul Cooke says the association's sole intention regarding the Republic of Ireland's recent UEFA Nations League matches against Israel was to fulfil those fixtures and to act in the best interest of Irish football, while not overlooking the situation in Gaza. Cooke was addressing delegates at the FAI's annual general meeting which was held in Cork on Saturday morning. He also spoke about the association's most recent invitation to attend the Oireachtas Committee on Sport next week to discuss safeguarding issues, and confirmed that the FAI will be unable to attend on the proposed date. Cooke detailed that they have offered to attend on several alternative dates and are happy to meet with members at a future agreed time. Committee chairman Alan Kelly TD has previously called on the Minister of State for Sport, Charlie McConalogue, to intervene if the FAI does not engage with the Committee. Packie Bonner, seeking to be ratified as an independent director, told the assembly that there had been a lot said around the Nations League games against Israel but that he stood by what he had previously stated at last year's AGM.

stories.title: Russian barrage hits Kyiv ahead of peace talks
stories.summary: Russian forces hammered energy infrastructure around Ukraine's capital with missiles and drones overnight, straining Kyiv's power supply and heating systems as temperatures headed towards zero, officials said. Three days before Russia and Ukraine are due to take part in US-brokered talks, explosions rocked Kyiv as Moscow unleashed waves of ballistic missiles, several of which hit and damaged the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Strikes on energy facilities outside Kyiv - including systems sending power from two nuclear plants to the city and Ukraine's central regions - caused serious damage, the energy ministry said, while at least two people were killed and around a dozen others wounded across Ukraine. "The capital is facing serious difficulties with its electricity, water, and heat supplies," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X, adding that substations in five other regions were also hit. He said Russia had launched 36 ballistic missiles, only four of which were intercepted, according to Ukraine's air force. It added that air defences had downed 149 out of 172 drones. "Russia is preparing for trilateral talks by launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine's critical infrastructure," Mr Zelensky said.

stories.title: Disco Pigs returns to Cork 30 years after debut
stories.summary: Disco Pigs, written by Enda Walsh, first hit the stage in Cork in 1996 and now it is back in its hometown on the stage at The Everyman theatre. Three decades on from that ground-breaking production, Tony Award-winning playwright Enda Walsh has returned to Cork to direct a new production of his play for the very first time, marking the show's anniversary. The play is notable in the history of Irish theatre as it launched the careers of the two leads, Cillian Murphy and Eileen Walsh, and Enda Walsh himself. "The idea of doing a theatre show of an old piece and reconnecting with that just felt like the right thing to do," playwright Enda Walsh said about his decision to revive the piece. Walsh explained that while the play has travelled to theatres across the world, this is his first time in the director's seat and that he has been hugely enjoying revisiting the show. "Part of me was like, I wanted to be in Cork and to go back to that play and to look at yourself you know, as a younger man," he said.
